+# Cube root of a 2x2 real-valued matrix with complex conjugate eigenvalues and equal diagonal values.
+# Reference [1]: Smith, M. I. (2003). A Schur Algorithm for Computing Matrix pth Roots.
+#   SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications (Vol. 24, Issue 4, pp. 971–989).
+#   https://doi.org/10.1137/s0895479801392697
+function _cbrt_2x2!(A::AbstractMatrix{T}) where {T<:Real}
+    m, n = size(A)
+    (m == 2 && n == 2) || throw(ArgumentError("_cbrt_2x2!: Matrix A must be 2x2."))
+    (A[1,1] == A[2,2]) || throw(ArgumentError("_cbrt_2x2!: Matrix A must have equal diagonal values."))
+    (A[1,2]*A[2,1] < 0) || throw(ArgumentError("_cbrt_2x2!: Matrix A must have complex conjugate eigenvalues."))
+    μ = sqrt(-4*A[1,2]*A[2,1])/2
+    r = cbrt(sqrt(A[1,1]^2 + μ^2))
+    θ = atan(μ, A[1,1])
+    α = r*cos(θ/3)
+    β′ = r*sin(θ/3)/µ
+    A[1,1] = α
+    A[2,2] = α
+    A[1,2] = β′*A[1,2]
+    A[2,1] = β′*A[2,1]
+    return A
+end
+
+# Cube root of a block diagonal matrix with 1x1 and 2x2 blocks (output of Schur decomposition)
+function _cbrt_blkdiag_1x1_2x2!(A::AbstractMatrix{T}) where {T<:Real}
+    m, n = size(A)
+    (m == n) || throw(ArgumentError("_cbrt_blkdiag_1x1_2x2!: Matrix A must be square."))
+    # 2x2 and 1x1 blocks
+    I₂ = findall(x -> !iszero(x), diag(A,-1))
+    I₁ = setdiff(1:n, vcat(I₂, I₂.+1))
+    for i in I₂ @views _cbrt_2x2!(A[i:i+1,i:i+1]) end
+    for i in I₁ @views A[i,i] = cbrt(A[i,i]) end
+    return A, I₂, I₁
+end

PR is the solution for #47513.
Baseline: 1.10.0-alpha1

# Summary of the Implementation
1. `cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix)` is delegated to `A^(1//3)`.
2. For real-valued `Diagonal` and `Symmetric` matrices, straightforward implementations based on scalar `cbrt` and `eigen` are provided.
3. For real-valued arbitrary matrices, a `schur` decomposition and [1, Algorithm 4.3]-based algorithm (`_cbrt_quasi_triu!`) is provided.
4. For real-valued upper and lower triangular matrices, straightforward solutions based on `_cbrt_quasi_triu!` are provided.

Note: See comment below for details on the algorithm.

## References
|  |   |
| ---- | ---- |
| [1]   | Smith, M. I. (2003). A Schur Algorithm for Computing Matrix pth Roots. In SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications (Vol. 24, Issue 4, pp. 971–989). https://doi.org/10.1137/s0895479801392697 |

# Tests
File: `stdlib/LinearAlgebra/test/dense.jl`
Testset: `@testset "cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix{T})"` 

```julia
Test Summary:              | Pass  Total  Time
```

# Memory and MIPS
```julia
julia> A = randn(1000,1000) ;
julia> @btime cbrt(A) ;
  793.222 ms (246051 allocations: 47.96 MiB)
julia> @btime A^(1//3) ;
  5.448 s (154 allocations: 900.61 MiB)
julia> @btime sqrt(A) ;
  894.408 ms (24 allocations: 91.86 MiB)
```

- Target was to get lower than `sqrt` wrt MIPS and memory consumption, which is done now 🎉🎉🎉

PR is the solution for #47513.
Baseline: 1.10.0-alpha1

# Summary of the Implementation
1. `cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix)` is delegated to `A^(1//3)`.
2. For real-valued `Diagonal` and `Symmetric` matrices, straightforward implementations based on scalar `cbrt` and `eigen` are provided.
3. For real-valued arbitrary matrices, a `schur` decomposition and [1, Algorithm 4.3]-based algorithm (`_cbrt_quasi_triu!`) is provided.
4. For real-valued upper and lower triangular matrices, straightforward solutions based on `_cbrt_quasi_triu!` are provided.

Note: See comment below for details on the algorithm.

## References
|  |   |
| ---- | ---- |
| [1]   | Smith, M. I. (2003). A Schur Algorithm for Computing Matrix pth Roots. In SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications (Vol. 24, Issue 4, pp. 971–989). https://doi.org/10.1137/s0895479801392697 |

# Pending Items
- [X] ~~Memory and MIPS optimisations (trade-off) for `_cbrt_quasi_triu!`.~~

# Tests
File: `stdlib/LinearAlgebra/test/dense.jl`
Testset: `@testset "cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix{T})"` 

```julia
Test Summary:              | Pass  Total  Time
cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix{T}) |   24     24  0.0s
```

# Memory and MIPS
```julia
julia> A = randn(1000,1000) ;
julia> @btime cbrt(A) ;
  793.222 ms (246051 allocations: 47.96 MiB)
julia> @btime A^(1//3) ;
  5.448 s (154 allocations: 900.61 MiB)
julia> @btime sqrt(A) ;
  894.408 ms (24 allocations: 91.86 MiB)
```

- Target was to get lower than `sqrt` wrt MIPS and memory consumption, which is done now 🎉🎉🎉

PR is the solution for #47513.
Baseline: 1.10.0-alpha1

# Summary of the Implementation
1. `cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix)` is delegated to `A^(1//3)`.
2. For real-valued `Diagonal` and `Symmetric` matrices, straightforward implementations based on scalar `cbrt` and `eigen` are provided.
3. For real-valued arbitrary matrices, a `schur` decomposition and [1, Algorithm 4.3]-based algorithm (`_cbrt_quasi_triu!`) is provided.
4. For real-valued upper and lower triangular matrices, straightforward solutions based on `_cbrt_quasi_triu!` are provided.

Note: See comment below for details on the algorithm.

## References
|  |   |
| ---- | ---- |
| [1]   | Smith, M. I. (2003). A Schur Algorithm for Computing Matrix pth Roots. In SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications (Vol. 24, Issue 4, pp. 971–989). https://doi.org/10.1137/s0895479801392697 |

# Pending Items
- [X] ~~Memory and MIPS optimisations (trade-off) for `_cbrt_quasi_triu!`.~~

# Tests
File: `stdlib/LinearAlgebra/test/dense.jl`
Testset: `@testset "cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix{T})"` 

```julia
Test Summary:              | Pass  Total  Time
cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix{T}) |   24     24  0.0s
```

# Memory and MIPS
```julia
julia> A = randn(1000,1000) ;
julia> @btime cbrt(A) ;
  793.222 ms (246051 allocations: 47.96 MiB)
julia> @btime A^(1//3) ;
  5.448 s (154 allocations: 900.61 MiB)
julia> @btime sqrt(A) ;
  894.408 ms (24 allocations: 91.86 MiB)
```

- Target was to get lower than `sqrt` wrt MIPS and memory consumption, which is done now 🎉🎉🎉

PR is the solution for #47513.
Baseline: 1.10.0-alpha1

# Summary of the Implementation
1. `cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix)` is delegated to `A^(1//3)`.
2. For real-valued `Diagonal` and `Symmetric` matrices, straightforward implementations based on scalar `cbrt` and `eigen` are provided.
3. For real-valued arbitrary matrices, a `schur` decomposition and [1, Algorithm 4.3]-based algorithm (`_cbrt_quasi_triu!`) is provided.
4. For real-valued upper and lower triangular matrices, straightforward solutions based on `_cbrt_quasi_triu!` are provided.

Note: See comment below for details on the algorithm.

## References
|  |   |
| ---- | ---- |
| [1]   | Smith, M. I. (2003). A Schur Algorithm for Computing Matrix pth Roots. In SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications (Vol. 24, Issue 4, pp. 971–989). https://doi.org/10.1137/s0895479801392697 |

# Pending Items
- [X] ~~Memory and MIPS optimisations (trade-off) for `_cbrt_quasi_triu!`.~~

# Tests
File: `stdlib/LinearAlgebra/test/dense.jl`
Testset: `@testset "cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix{T})"` 

```julia
Test Summary:              | Pass  Total  Time
cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix{T}) |   24     24  0.0s
```

# Memory and MIPS
```julia
julia> A = randn(1000,1000) ;
julia> @btime cbrt(A) ;
  793.222 ms (246051 allocations: 47.96 MiB)
julia> @btime A^(1//3) ;
  5.448 s (154 allocations: 900.61 MiB)
julia> @btime sqrt(A) ;
  894.408 ms (24 allocations: 91.86 MiB)
```

- Target was to get lower than `sqrt` wrt MIPS and memory consumption, which is done now 🎉🎉🎉

 sqrt(A::AdjointAbsMat) = adjoint(sqrt(parent(A)))
 sqrt(A::TransposeAbsMat) = transpose(sqrt(parent(A)))
 
+# Cube root for complex-valued matrices
+cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix) = A^(1//3)
+
+# Cube root for real valued matrices
+function cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix{T}) where {T<:Real}
+    if checksquare(A) == 0
+        return copy(A)
+    elseif issymmetric(A)
+        return cbrt(Symmetric(A, :U))
+    else
+        S = schur(A)
+        return S.Z * _cbrt_quasi_triu!(S.T) * S.Z'
+    end
+end

PR is the solution for #47513.
Baseline: 1.10.0-alpha1

# Summary of the Implementation
1. `cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix)` is delegated to `A^(1//3)`.
2. For real-valued `Diagonal` and `Symmetric` matrices, straightforward implementations based on scalar `cbrt` and `eigen` are provided.
3. For real-valued arbitrary matrices, a `schur` decomposition and [1, Algorithm 4.3]-based algorithm (`_cbrt_quasi_triu!`) is provided.
4. For real-valued upper and lower triangular matrices, straightforward solutions based on `_cbrt_quasi_triu!` are provided.

Note: See comment below for details on the algorithm.

## References
|  |   |
| ---- | ---- |
| [1]   | Smith, M. I. (2003). A Schur Algorithm for Computing Matrix pth Roots. In SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications (Vol. 24, Issue 4, pp. 971–989). https://doi.org/10.1137/s0895479801392697 |

```julia
  894.408 ms (24 allocations: 91.86 MiB)
```

PR is the solution for #47513.
Baseline: 1.10.0-alpha1

# Summary of the Implementation
1. `cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix)` is delegated to `A^(1//3)`.
2. For real-valued `Diagonal` and `Symmetric` matrices, straightforward implementations based on scalar `cbrt` and `eigen` are provided.
3. For real-valued arbitrary matrices, a `schur` decomposition and [1, Algorithm 4.3]-based algorithm (`_cbrt_quasi_triu!`) is provided.
4. For real-valued upper and lower triangular matrices, straightforward solutions based on `_cbrt_quasi_triu!` are provided.

Note: See comment below for details on the algorithm.

## References
|  |   |
| ---- | ---- |
| [1]   | Smith, M. I. (2003). A Schur Algorithm for Computing Matrix pth Roots. In SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications (Vol. 24, Issue 4, pp. 971–989). https://doi.org/10.1137/s0895479801392697 |

# Pending Items
- [X] ~~Memory and MIPS optimisations (trade-off) for `_cbrt_quasi_triu!`.~~

# Tests
File: `stdlib/LinearAlgebra/test/dense.jl`
Testset: `@testset "cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix{T})"` 

```julia
Test Summary:              | Pass  Total  Time
cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix{T}) |   24     24  0.0s
```

# Memory and MIPS
```julia
julia> A = randn(1000,1000) ;
julia> @btime cbrt(A) ;
  793.222 ms (246051 allocations: 47.96 MiB)
julia> @btime A^(1//3) ;
  5.448 s (154 allocations: 900.61 MiB)
julia> @btime sqrt(A) ;
  894.408 ms (24 allocations: 91.86 MiB)
```

- Target was to get lower than `sqrt` wrt MIPS and memory consumption, which is done now 🎉🎉🎉

PR is the solution for #47513.
Baseline: 1.10.0-alpha1

# Summary of the Implementation
1. `cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix)` is delegated to `A^(1//3)`.
2. For real-valued `Diagonal` and `Symmetric` matrices, straightforward implementations based on scalar `cbrt` and `eigen` are provided.
3. For real-valued arbitrary matrices, a `schur` decomposition and [1, Algorithm 4.3]-based algorithm (`_cbrt_quasi_triu!`) is provided.
4. For real-valued upper and lower triangular matrices, straightforward solutions based on `_cbrt_quasi_triu!` are provided.

Note: See comment below for details on the algorithm.

## References
|  |   |
| ---- | ---- |
| [1]   | Smith, M. I. (2003). A Schur Algorithm for Computing Matrix pth Roots. In SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications (Vol. 24, Issue 4, pp. 971–989). https://doi.org/10.1137/s0895479801392697 |

# Pending Items
- [X] ~~Memory and MIPS optimisations (trade-off) for `_cbrt_quasi_triu!`.~~

# Tests
File: `stdlib/LinearAlgebra/test/dense.jl`
Testset: `@testset "cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix{T})"` 

```julia
Test Summary:              | Pass  Total  Time
cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix{T}) |   24     24  0.0s
```

# Memory and MIPS
```julia
julia> A = randn(1000,1000) ;
julia> @btime cbrt(A) ;
  793.222 ms (246051 allocations: 47.96 MiB)
julia> @btime A^(1//3) ;
  5.448 s (154 allocations: 900.61 MiB)
julia> @btime sqrt(A) ;
  894.408 ms (24 allocations: 91.86 MiB)
```

- Target was to get lower than `sqrt` wrt MIPS and memory consumption, which is done now 🎉🎉🎉

PR is the solution for #47513.
Baseline: 1.10.0-alpha1

# Summary of the Implementation
1. `cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix)` is delegated to `A^(1//3)`.
2. For real-valued `Diagonal` and `Symmetric` matrices, straightforward implementations based on scalar `cbrt` and `eigen` are provided.
3. For real-valued arbitrary matrices, a `schur` decomposition and [1, Algorithm 4.3]-based algorithm (`_cbrt_quasi_triu!`) is provided.
4. For real-valued upper and lower triangular matrices, straightforward solutions based on `_cbrt_quasi_triu!` are provided.

Note: See comment below for details on the algorithm.

## References
|  |   |
| ---- | ---- |
| [1]   | Smith, M. I. (2003). A Schur Algorithm for Computing Matrix pth Roots. In SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications (Vol. 24, Issue 4, pp. 971–989). https://doi.org/10.1137/s0895479801392697 |

# Pending Items
- [X] ~~Memory and MIPS optimisations (trade-off) for `_cbrt_quasi_triu!`.~~

# Tests
File: `stdlib/LinearAlgebra/test/dense.jl`
Testset: `@testset "cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix{T})"` 

```julia
Test Summary:              | Pass  Total  Time
cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix{T}) |   24     24  0.0s
```

# Memory and MIPS
```julia
julia> A = randn(1000,1000) ;
julia> @btime cbrt(A) ;
  793.222 ms (246051 allocations: 47.96 MiB)
julia> @btime A^(1//3) ;
  5.448 s (154 allocations: 900.61 MiB)
julia> @btime sqrt(A) ;
  894.408 ms (24 allocations: 91.86 MiB)
```

- Target was to get lower than `sqrt` wrt MIPS and memory consumption, which is done now 🎉🎉🎉

PR is the solution for #47513.
Baseline: 1.10.0-alpha1

# Summary of the Implementation
1. `cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix)` is delegated to `A^(1//3)`.
2. For real-valued `Diagonal` and `Symmetric` matrices, straightforward implementations based on scalar `cbrt` and `eigen` are provided.
3. For real-valued arbitrary matrices, a `schur` decomposition and [1, Algorithm 4.3]-based algorithm (`_cbrt_quasi_triu!`) is provided.
4. For real-valued upper and lower triangular matrices, straightforward solutions based on `_cbrt_quasi_triu!` are provided.

Note: See comment below for details on the algorithm.

## References
|  |   |
| ---- | ---- |
| [1]   | Smith, M. I. (2003). A Schur Algorithm for Computing Matrix pth Roots. In SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications (Vol. 24, Issue 4, pp. 971–989). https://doi.org/10.1137/s0895479801392697 |

# Pending Items
- [X] ~~Memory and MIPS optimisations (trade-off) for `_cbrt_quasi_triu!`.~~

# Tests
File: `stdlib/LinearAlgebra/test/dense.jl`
Testset: `@testset "cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix{T})"` 

```julia
Test Summary:              | Pass  Total  Time
cbrt(A::AbstractMatrix{T}) |   24     24  0.0s
```

# Memory and MIPS
```julia
julia> A = randn(1000,1000) ;
julia> @btime cbrt(A) ;
  793.222 ms (246051 allocations: 47.96 MiB)
julia> @btime A^(1//3) ;
  5.448 s (154 allocations: 900.61 MiB)
julia> @btime sqrt(A) ;
  894.408 ms (24 allocations: 91.86 MiB)
```

- Target was to get lower than `sqrt` wrt MIPS and memory consumption, which is done now 🎉🎉🎉

Introduction

This PR implements Bunchkaufman (BK)-decomposition based generalized eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $\boldsymbol{A}$ and $\boldsymbol{B}$ when $\boldsymbol{A}$ is arbitrary and $\boldsymbol{B}$ is (Hermitian) symmetric in the following new methods in `stdlib/LinearAlgebra/src/symmetriceigen.jl`:
1. Function `eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, B::BunchKaufman{T,<:StridedMatrix}; sortby)`
2. In-place version: `eigvals!(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, B::BunchKaufman{T,<:StridedMatrix}; sortby)`
3. Function `eigen(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, B::BunchKaufman{T,<:StridedMatrix}; sortby)`
4. In-place version: `eigen!(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, B::BunchKaufman{T,<:StridedMatrix}; sortby)`

The implemention uses `LinearAlgebra.LAPACK` and, for most cases, **outperforms the equivalent native (`eigen.jl`) functions** in both execution time and memory usage for $N\geq 32.$ Test and benchmark results will be [updated here regularly](https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/pull/50471#issuecomment-1627088845).

Comments are suggestions are welcome.

- Note 1: No direct LAPACK functions for $\boldsymbol{A}$ arbitrary and $\boldsymbol{B}$ (Hermitian) symmetric presently exist. However, this implementation could be a basis for one, if desired.
- Note 2: This work is an overspill from PR #49673. The comments there may also be relevant for this PR.

# Open points
- [ ] `bunchkaufman.jl`'s `getproperty` creates copies for each call to obtain `D` and `L/U`. Hence, an equivalent in-place implementation is supplied. To be checked if code duplication between `bunchkaufman.jl` and `symmetriceigen.jl` can be avoided.
- [ ] `dense.jl`'s `eigen!` creates copies when having complex-valued eigenvectors for real-valued matrices -> This causes additional memory consumption for real-valued matrices, see case `N=1000/R/BK/E!` in benchmark results below.
- [ ] Check why `dl` and `du` memory locations are not allowed to be aliased in `LAPACK.gtsv!`.

`symmetriceigen.jl` file was (possibly) written to take advantage of LAPACK's low-complexity [X]SY[YYY] class of functions, which compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors for symmetric and Hermitian symmetric matrices, see [blame symmetriceigen.jl](https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/blame/master/stdlib/LinearAlgebra/src/symmetriceigen.jl). The same class of functions also support computing generalised eigenvalues and eigenvectors for two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$.

However, there are no LAPACK routines for the case when one of $A$ and $B$ is not (Hemitian or) symmetric. **Thus, I feel that the functions for such combinations are best delegated to their "non-symmetric" (usual) counterparts.**

Cumulatively, #49533 reports two problems (one initially and one in further comments):
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The `eigen!(A,B)` for the same case, i.e., when one of `A` or `B` is not symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition instead of delegating the call. The issue with using Cholesky decomposition is that it is not defined for Hermitian (or symmetric) matrices but only for positive (semi-) definite matrices, causing the function fail for a large number of inputs.

**This PR contains the following changes:**

1. Wire `eig/en/vals(A,Symmmetric/Hermitian(B))` and `eig/en/vals(Symmmetric/Hermitian(A), B)` (only one of the matrices is symmetric/Hermitian) to the "plain" LAPACK versions without any optimization for the symmetry.
2. Implement (reuse `eigen`) `eig/en/vals(A, cholesky(B))` when $B$ is positive definite and its Cholesky decomposition is passed in the second argument. In this case, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `cholesky(B).U`). Is this misleading?
3. Implement `eig/en/vals(A, bunchkaufman(B))` when $B$ is indefinite symmetric or Hermitian. Again, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `bunchkaufman(B).U/.L`). Is this misleading?

> This seems like a reasonable approach, and the low-rank case is perhaps undefined behavior? 

For this case, MATLAB and Mathematica produce infinites. Personally, I'd prefer that too. However, `eigvals(A,B)` for generic matrices produces `NaN`. I'm not sure why this decision was taken.

> Also, how does the Bunch-Kaufman approach compare with Cholesky, for positive-definite cases? 

```julia
julia> A,B = mm(1000) ;
julia> BP = B*B' ;
julia> @btime eigvals(A,BP) ;
  4.901 s (16 allocations: 33.62 MiB)
julia> @btime eigvals(A,bunchkaufman(BP)) ;
  953.674 ms (42 allocations: 108.48 MiB)
julia> @btime eigvals(A,cholesky(BP)) ;
  964.962 ms (19 allocations: 46.33 MiB)

julia> @btime eigen(A,BP) ;
  6.208 s (19 allocations: 48.87 MiB)
julia> @btime eigen(A,bunchkaufman(BP)) ;
  1.376 s (63 allocations: 171.01 MiB)
julia> @btime eigen(A,cholesky(BP)) ;
  1.420 s (34 allocations: 78.34 MiB)
```

This is in-line with my expectation: LDLT (Bunchkaufman) and Cholesky are roughly of the same computational complexity. However, BK is more memory intensive. Kindly let me know if my code is suboptimal wrt memory. I feel that the routine can be speeded up if `SymTridiagonal` can properly support Hermitian matrices (currently buggy) and `bunchkaufman` returns a `SymTridiagonal` instead of a `Tridiagonal`. (Or a new `HermTridiagonal` is created).

Side rant: One of the reasons I started doing this public domain work is because my colleagues derided Julia due to its poor and unstable Linear Algebra support. It's come a long way since earlier, but still has to go quite far. Also, am not sure if Linear Algebra exploits the type system fully.

> Would it be possible for `eigvals(A, B::Symmetric)` to call `eigvals(A, bunchkaufman(B))` internally if the low-rank issue is addressed? Is performance the only concern, in that case?

Indeed, performance is the only concern. For anything under $N=1000$ the LAPACK routines are much faster. However, it will be interesting to understand the bottleneck of Julia->LAPACK routines for large matrices, and if anything can be done about that (i.e., is it purely computational or also memory, etc?).
 
> If we decide to go this route, should we (is a separate PR) add similar methods for the single-argument positive-definite case as well? E.g. something like [SPTEQR](https://netlib.org/lapack/explore-html/d1/ddc/group__real_p_tcomputational_ga72b5ecbbf9359796ae9368a141d2540c.html)

Sounds good.

Sometimes it's useful to compute just a single eigenvector (e.g. by the power method), and any eigenvector will do, e.g. I have an irreducible Markov chain, where the eigenvector is unique. I couldn't find any functions for this; should we add one to `LinearAlgebra`?

If your matrix is symmetric, kindly take a look at `eigen(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm, irange::UnitRange)` in `symmetriceigen.jl`, which can optionally return a single eigenvalue and associated eigenvector. It uses LAPACK's XSYEVR, which is quite efficient.

> Huh, that's surprising, I thought the power method was still standard for the largest eigenvalue problem.

If deemed sufficient, a basic version of the power algorithm can be easily implemented by users themselves. Please take a look at the code in https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/pull/49487 (mentioned in the earlier comments) for an example implementation. I feel it might be a great idea to add this algorithm to the Julia documentation.

`symmetriceigen.jl` file was (possibly) written to take advantage of LAPACK's low-complexity [X]SY[YYY] class of functions, which compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors for symmetric and Hermitian symmetric matrices, see [blame symmetriceigen.jl](https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/blame/master/stdlib/LinearAlgebra/src/symmetriceigen.jl). The same class of functions also support computing generalised eigenvalues and eigenvectors for two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$.

However, there are no LAPACK routines for the case when one of $A$ and $B$ is not (Hemitian or) symmetric. **Thus, I feel that the functions for such combinations are best delegated to their "non-symmetric" (usual) counterparts.**

Cumulatively, #49533 reports two problems (one initially and one in further comments):
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The `eigen!(A,B)` for the same case, i.e., when one of `A` or `B` is not symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition instead of delegating the call. The issue with using Cholesky decomposition is that it is not defined for Hermitian (or symmetric) matrices but only for positive (semi-) definite matrices, causing the function fail for a large number of inputs.

**This PR contains the following changes:**

1. Wire `eig/en/vals(A,Symmmetric/Hermitian(B))` and `eig/en/vals(Symmmetric/Hermitian(A), B)` (only one of the matrices is symmetric/Hermitian) to the "plain" LAPACK versions without any optimization for the symmetry.
2. Implement (reuse `eigen`) `eig/en/vals(A, cholesky(B))` when $B$ is positive definite and its Cholesky decomposition is passed in the second argument. In this case, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `cholesky(B).U`). Is this misleading?
3. Implement `eig/en/vals(A, bunchkaufman(B))` when $B$ is indefinite symmetric or Hermitian. Again, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `bunchkaufman(B).U/.L`). Is this misleading?

`symmetriceigen.jl` file was (possibly) written to take advantage of LAPACK's low-complexity [X]SY[YYY] class of functions, which compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors for symmetric and Hermitian symmetric matrices, see [blame symmetriceigen.jl](https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/blame/master/stdlib/LinearAlgebra/src/symmetriceigen.jl). The same class of functions also support computing generalised eigenvalues and eigenvectors for two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$.

However, there are no LAPACK routines for the case when one of $A$ and $B$ is not (Hemitian or) symmetric. **Thus, I feel that the functions for such combinations are best delegated to their "non-symmetric" (usual) counterparts.**

Cumulatively, #49533 reports two problems (one initially and one in further comments):
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The `eigen!(A,B)` for the same case, i.e., when one of `A` or `B` is not symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition instead of delegating the call. The issue with using Cholesky decomposition is that it is not defined for Hermitian (or symmetric) matrices but only for positive (semi-) definite matrices, causing the function fail for a large number of inputs.

**This PR contains the following changes:**

1. Wire `eig/en/vals(A,Symmmetric/Hermitian(B))` and `eig/en/vals(Symmmetric/Hermitian(A), B)` (only one of the matrices is symmetric/Hermitian) to the "plain" LAPACK versions without any optimization for the symmetry.
2. Implement (reuse `eigen`) `eig/en/vals(A, cholesky(B))` when $B$ is positive definite and its Cholesky decomposition is passed in the second argument. In this case, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `cholesky(B).U`). Is this misleading?

`symmetriceigen.jl` file was (possibly) written to take advantage of LAPACK's low-complexity [X]SY[YYY] class of functions, which compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors for symmetric and Hermitian symmetric matrices, see [blame symmetriceigen.jl](https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/blame/master/stdlib/LinearAlgebra/src/symmetriceigen.jl). The same class of functions also support computing generalised eigenvalues and eigenvectors for two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$.

However, there are no LAPACK routines for the case when one of $A$ and $B$ is not (Hemitian or) symmetric. **Thus, I feel that the functions for such combinations are best delegated to their "non-symmetric" (usual) counterparts.**

Cumulatively, #49533 reports two problems (one initially and one in further comments):
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The `eigen!(A,B)` for the same case, i.e., when one of `A` or `B` is not symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition instead of delegating the call. The issue with using Cholesky decomposition is that it is not defined for Hermitian (or symmetric) matrices but only for positive (semi-) definite matrices, causing the function fail for a large number of inputs.

**This PR contains the following changes:**

1. Wire `eig/en/vals(A,Symmmetric/Hermitian(B))` and `eig/en/vals(Symmmetric/Hermitian(A), B)` (only one of the matrices is symmetric/Hermitian) to the "plain" LAPACK versions without any optimization for the symmetry.
2. Implement (reuse `eigen`) `eig/en/vals(A, cholesky(B))` when $B$ is positive definite and its Cholesky decomposition is passed in the second argument. In this case, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `cholesky(B).U`). Is this misleading?
3. Implement `eig/en/vals(A, bunchkaufman(B))` when $B$ is indefinite symmetric or Hermitian. Again, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `bunchkaufman(B).U/.L`). Is this misleading?

`symmetriceigen.jl` file was (possibly) written to take advantage of LAPACK's low-complexity [X]SY[YYY] class of functions, which compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors for symmetric and Hermitian symmetric matrices, see [blame symmetriceigen.jl](https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/blame/master/stdlib/LinearAlgebra/src/symmetriceigen.jl). The same class of functions also support computing generalised eigenvalues and eigenvectors for two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$.

However, there are no LAPACK routines for the case when one of $A$ and $B$ is not (Hemitian or) symmetric. **Thus, I feel that the functions for such combinations are best delegated to their "non-symmetric" (usual) counterparts.**

Cumulatively, #49533 reports two problems (one initially and one in further comments):
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The `eigen!(A,B)` for the same case, i.e., when one of `A` or `B` is not symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition instead of delegating the call. The issue with using Cholesky decomposition is that it is not defined for Hermitian (or symmetric) matrices but only for positive (semi-) definite matrices, causing the function fail for a large number of inputs.

**This PR contains the following changes:**

1. Wire `eig/en/vals(A,Symmmetric/Hermitian(B))` and `eig/en/vals(Symmmetric/Hermitian(A), B)` (only one of the matrices is symmetric/Hermitian) to the "plain" LAPACK versions without any optimization for the symmetry.
2. Implement (reuse `eigen`) `eig/en/vals(A, cholesky(B))` when $B$ is positive definite and its Cholesky decomposition is passed in the second argument. In this case, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `cholesky(B).U`). Is this misleading?
3. Implement `eig/en/vals(A, bunchkaufman(B))` when $B$ is indefinite symmetric or Hermitian. Again, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `bunchkaufman(B).U/.L`). Is this misleading?

However, there are no LAPACK routines for the case when one of $A$ and $B$ is not (Hemitian or) symmetric. **Thus, I feel that the functions for such combinations are best delegated to their "non-symmetric" (usual) counterparts.**

Cumulatively, #49533 reports two problems (one initially and one in further comments):

**This PR contains the following changes:**

2. Implement (reuse `eigen`) `eig/en/vals(A, cholesky(B))` when $B$ is positive definite and its Cholesky decomposition is passed in the second argument. In this case, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `cholesky(B).U`). Is this misleading?

The same class of functions also support computing generalised eigenvalues and eigenvectors for two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$.

However, there are no LAPACK routines for the case when one of $A$ and $B$ is not (Hemitian or) symmetric. **Thus, I feel that the functions for such combinations are best delegated to their "non-symmetric" (usual) counterparts.**

Cumulatively, #49533 reports two problems (one initially and one in further comments):
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The `eigen!(A,B)` for the same case, i.e., when one of `A` or `B` is not symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition instead of delegating the call. The issue with using Cholesky decomposition is that it is not defined for Hermitian (or symmetric) matrices but only for positive (semi-) definite matrices, causing the function fail for a large number of inputs.

**This PR contains the following changes:**

1. Wire `eig/en/vals(A,Symmmetric/Hermitian(B))` and `eig/en/vals(Symmmetric/Hermitian(A), B)` (only one of the matrices is symmetric/Hermitian) to the "plain" LAPACK versions without any optimization for the symmetry.
2. Implement (reuse `eigen`) `eig/en/vals(A, cholesky(B))` when $B$ is positive definite and its Cholesky decomposition is passed in the second argument. In this case, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `cholesky(B).U`). Is this misleading?
3. Implement `eig/en/vals(A, bunchkaufman(B))` when $B$ is indefinite symmetric or Hermitian. Again, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `bunchkaufman(B).U/.L`). Is this misleading?

The same class of functions also support computing generalised eigenvalues and eigenvectors for two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$.

However, there are no LAPACK routines for the case when one of $A$ and $B$ is not (Hemitian or) symmetric. **Thus, I feel that the functions for such combinations are best delegated to their "non-symmetric" (usual) counterparts.**

Cumulatively, #49533 reports two problems (one initially and one in further comments):
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The `eigen!(A,B)` for the same case, i.e., when one of `A` or `B` is not symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition instead of delegating the call. The issue with using Cholesky decomposition is that it is not defined for Hermitian (or symmetric) matrices but only for positive (semi-) definite matrices, causing the function fail for a large number of inputs.

**This PR contains the following changes:**

1. Wire `eig/en/vals(A,Symmmetric/Hermitian(B))` and `eig/en/vals(Symmmetric/Hermitian(A), B)` (only one of the matrices is symmetric/Hermitian) to the "plain" LAPACK versions without any optimization for the symmetry.

`symmetriceigen.jl` file was (possibly) written to take advantage of LAPACK's low-complexity [X]SY[YYY] class of functions, which compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors for symmetric and Hermitian symmetric matrices, see [blame symmetriceigen.jl](https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/blame/master/stdlib/LinearAlgebra/src/symmetriceigen.jl). The same class of functions also support computing generalised eigenvalues and eigenvectors for two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$.

However, there are no LAPACK routines for the case when one of $A$ and $B$ is not (Hemitian or) symmetric. **Thus, I feel that the functions for such combinations are best delegated to their "non-symmetric" (usual) counterparts.**

Cumulatively, #49533 reports two problems (one initially and one in further comments):
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The `eigen!(A,B)` for the same case, i.e., when one of `A` or `B` is not symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition instead of delegating the call. The issue with using Cholesky decomposition is that it is not defined for Hermitian (or symmetric) matrices but only for positive (semi-) definite matrices, causing the function fail for a large number of inputs.

**This PR contains the following changes:**

1. Wire `eig/en/vals(A,Symmmetric/Hermitian(B))` and `eig/en/vals(Symmmetric/Hermitian(A), B)` (only one of the matrices is symmetric/Hermitian) to the "plain" LAPACK versions without any optimization for the symmetry.
2. Implement (reuse `eigen`) `eig/en/vals(A, cholesky(B))` when $B$ is positive definite and its Cholesky decomposition is passed in the second argument. In this case, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `cholesky(B).U`). Is this misleading?
3. Implement `eig/en/vals(A, bunchkaufman(B))` when $B$ is indefinite symmetric or Hermitian. Again, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `bunchkaufman(B).U/.L`). Is this misleading?

`symmetriceigen.jl` file was (possibly) written to take advantage of LAPACK's low-complexity [X]SY[YYY] class of functions, which compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors for symmetric and Hermitian symmetric matrices, see [blame symmetriceigen.jl](https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/blame/master/stdlib/LinearAlgebra/src/symmetriceigen.jl). The same class of functions also support computing generalised eigenvalues and eigenvectors for two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$.

However, there are no LAPACK routines for the case when one of $A$ and $B$ is not (Hemitian or) symmetric. **Thus, I feel that the functions for such combinations are best delegated to their "non-symmetric" (usual) counterparts.**

Cumulatively, #49533 reports two problems (one initially and one in further comments):
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The `eigen!(A,B)` for the same case, i.e., when one of `A` or `B` is not symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition instead of delegating the call. The issue with using Cholesky decomposition is that it is not defined for Hermitian (or symmetric) matrices but only for positive (semi-) definite matrices, causing the function fail for a large number of inputs.

**This PR contains the following changes:**

1. Wire `eig/en/vals(A,Symmmetric/Hermitian(B))` and `eig/en/vals(Symmmetric/Hermitian(A), B)` (only one of the matrices is symmetric/Hermitian) to the "plain" LAPACK versions without any optimization for the symmetry.
2. Implement (reuse `eigen`) `eig/en/vals(A, cholesky(B))` when $B$ is positive definite and its Cholesky decomposition is passed in the second argument. In this case, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `cholesky(B).U`). Is this misleading?
3. Implement `eig/en/vals(A, bunchkaufman(B))` when $B$ is indefinite symmetric or Hermitian. Again, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `bunchkaufman(B).U/.L`). Is this misleading?

`symmetriceigen.jl` file was (possibly) written to take advantage of LAPACK's low-complexity [X]SY[YYY] class of functions, which compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors for symmetric and Hermitian symmetric matrices, see [blame symmetriceigen.jl](https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/blame/master/stdlib/LinearAlgebra/src/symmetriceigen.jl). The same class of functions also support computing generalised eigenvalues and eigenvectors for two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$.

However, there are no LAPACK routines for the case when one of $A$ and $B$ is not (Hemitian or) symmetric. **Thus, I feel that the functions for such combinations are best delegated to their "non-symmetric" (usual) counterparts.**

Cumulatively, #49533 reports two problems (one initially and one in further comments):
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The `eigen!(A,B)` for the same case, i.e., when one of `A` or `B` is not symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition instead of delegating the call. The issue with using Cholesky decomposition is that it is not defined for Hermitian (or symmetric) matrices but only for positive (semi-) definite matrices, causing the function fail for a large number of inputs.

**This PR contains the following changes:**

1. Wire `eig/en/vals(A,Symmmetric/Hermitian(B))` and `eig/en/vals(Symmmetric/Hermitian(A), B)` (only one of the matrices is symmetric/Hermitian) to the "plain" LAPACK versions without any optimization for the symmetry.

Dear @dkarrasch, firstly, I'd like to thank you for your valuable comments. Below, I try to provide my response, point-by-point for some of the aspects in your comments. The ones not mentioned here have been accepted, and a link to the commit IDs are provided in their comment response. Hope this is Ok.

> The in-place lu!(B.D) seems to be not working in the real symmetric case. 

Firstly, not finding this in unit testing was clearly an oversight on my end. Thank you for brining this to notice. The tests in `tests/symmetriceigen.jl` for BK only covered the complex-valued cases earlier. Now, in https://github.com/aravindh-krishnamoorthy/julia/commit/5c566b14ce81ce894b88b198b23befce84f52dfb, I have included cases for real-valued inputs for both BK and Cholesky. Please let me know in case you'd like more cases to be added.

The problem with `lu!(B.D)` is due to follows: In Bunch-Kaufmann's `getfield(B, :D)`, a `Tridiagonal` matrix is created in the lines:
```julia
if getfield(B, :uplo) == 'L'
    odl = od[1:n - 1]
    return Tridiagonal(odl, diag(LUD), getfield(B, :symmetric) ? odl : conj.(odl))
else # 'U'
    odu = od[2:n]
    return Tridiagonal(getfield(B, :symmetric) ? odu : conj.(odu), diag(LUD), odu)
end
```
which aliases the pointers for real-valued BK matrices (!). Whether this is a problem in itself is debatable. But, there is  incompatibility between the (aliased) return value of `getfield` of BK and the (unaliased) input requirement of `lu!()` (!)

To resolve this incompatibility in this PR, I've just made a copy of `B.D` in https://github.com/aravindh-krishnamoorthy/julia/commit/8361afab9a23a9b57ba8503cbdf6c4d6133325d2, which has negligible performance impact. Hope the fix is satisfactory.

> Also, is there a specific reason this function body is not simply move to eigen! a few lines above? I guess the same question applies to the cholesky case above. 

I've incorporated these changes. Kindly see the resolution comment in the review.

> And one more thing: this seems to be out-of-place w.r.t. A, right? Because A[B.p,B.p] allocates basically another copy of A. So I start to wonder what's the benefit of the whole BunchKaufman approach. Would views help here instead of slicing? Presumably UiAUti! will be much slower on views.

Indeed. As you rightly speculate, views are slower, perhaps due to the (symmetric) permutation being in both the columns and the rows, whose symmetry is not yet fully exploited to improve performance. However, creating a copy via `A[B.p, B.p]` did not seem to have a performance impact. Hence, I settled for this approach.

As seen from the performance reports in the comments above, BK is useful when the (Hermitian / symmetric) matrices are very large. This is analogous to the earlier code based on Cholesky decomposition, which is also only useful when the (Positive (semi) definite) matrices are very large. For small matrices, the naïve solution in the original commit is sufficient. (Note the the motivation for BK-based solution was that Cholesky-based solution is only applicable to positive definite matrices whereas the API is for symmetric matrices).

Kindly let me know if my resolution seems satisfactory. If so, I will resolve the open comment. Furthermore, if you suggest that the PR is ready, I can also make the corresponding documentation changes.

I look forward to your views.

`symmetriceigen.jl` file was (possibly) written to take advantage of LAPACK's low-complexity [X]SY[YYY] class of functions, which compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors for symmetric and Hermitian The same class of functions also support computing generalised eigenvalues and eigenvectors for two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$.

However, there are no LAPACK routines for the case when one of $A$ and $B$ is not (Hemitian or) symmetric. **Thus, I feel that the functions for such combinations are best delegated to their "non-symmetric" (usual) counterparts.**

Cumulatively, #49533 reports two problems (one initially and one in further comments):
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The `eigen!(A,B)` for the same case, i.e., when one of `A` or `B` is not symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition instead of delegating the call. The issue with using Cholesky decomposition is that it is not defined for Hermitian (or symmetric) matrices but only for positive (semi-) definite matrices, causing the function fail for a large number of inputs.

**This PR contains the following changes:**

1. Wire `eig/en/vals(A,Symmmetric/Hermitian(B))` and `eig/en/vals(Symmmetric/Hermitian(A), B)` (only one of the matrices is symmetric/Hermitian) to the "plain" LAPACK versions without any optimization for the symmetry.

3. Implement `eig/en/vals(A, bunchkaufman(B))` when $B$ is indefinite symmetric or Hermitian. Again, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `bunchkaufman(B).U/.L`). Is this misleading?

`symmetriceigen.jl` file was (possibly) written to take advantage of LAPACK's low-complexity [X]SY[YYY] class of functions, which compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors for symmetric and Hermitian symmetric matrices, see [blame symmetriceigen.jl](https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/blame/master/stdlib/LinearAlgebra/src/symmetriceigen.jl). The same class of functions also support computing generalised eigenvalues and eigenvectors for two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$.

However, there are no LAPACK routines for the case when one of $A$ and $B$ is not (Hemitian or) symmetric. **Thus, I feel that the functions for such combinations are best delegated to their "non-symmetric" (usual) counterparts.**

Cumulatively, #49533 reports two problems (one initially and one in further comments):
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The `eigen!(A,B)` for the same case, i.e., when one of `A` or `B` is not symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition instead of delegating the call. The issue with using Cholesky decomposition is that it is not defined for Hermitian (or symmetric) matrices but only for positive (semi-) definite matrices, causing the function fail for a large number of inputs.

**This PR contains the following changes:**

1. Wire `eig/en/vals(A,Symmmetric/Hermitian(B))` and `eig/en/vals(Symmmetric/Hermitian(A), B)` (only one of the matrices is symmetric/Hermitian) to the "plain" LAPACK versions without any optimization for the symmetry.
2. Implement (reuse `eigen`) `eig/en/vals(A, cholesky(B))` when $B$ is positive definite and its Cholesky decomposition is passed in the second argument. In this case, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `cholesky(B).U`). Is this misleading?
3. Implement `eig/en/vals(A, bunchkaufman(B))` when $B$ is indefinite symmetric or Hermitian. Again, `eig/en/vals` of $A$ and $B$ are computed (and not of $A$ and `bunchkaufman(B).U/.L`). Is this misleading?

This is not such an easy issue to work on unless you understand a fair amount of linear algebra. In particular, until you understand why `sqrt(A)` can't use eigenvalues for non-Hermitian matrices, and what it does instead, you won't understand this issue.
> 
> At _minimum_, you need to understand [this paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/002437958380010X?via%3Dihub) (which also gives a `cbrt` algorithm!) and [this code for `sqrt(A)`](https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/blob/0da46e25c865a390b5c2de20c2d40afb41fcac0a/stdlib/LinearAlgebra/src/dense.jl#L877-L903) and probably [this code for `A^p` too](https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/blob/0da46e25c865a390b5c2de20c2d40afb41fcac0a/stdlib/LinearAlgebra/src/dense.jl#L490-L521) before you can sensibly work on `cbrt(A)`.

Hello @stevengj, thank you for this valuable input. I have taken a look at the mentioned references: I'm aware of the paper [1] and I also reviewed the code for `sqrt(A)` and `A^p`. However, I'm not sure if I fully appreciate the hurdles you allude to in the post. I kindly request you to review my plan below and let me know if I've missed something.

1. Straightforward implementations to begin with the task:
1.1 Diagonal matrices: `cbrt :: Diagonal{T<:Union{Real,Complex}} -> Diagonal{T}`, can be made type stable.
1.2 Symmetric matrices: `cbrt :: Symmetric{T<:Real} -> Symmetric{T<:Real}`, can be made type stable.
1.3 Hermitian-symmetric matrices: `cbrt :: Hermitian{T<:Complex} -> Hermitian{T<:Complex}`, type stable. 

2. Arbitrary complex-valued matrices:
2.1 Using Schur decomposition: `cbrt :: AbstractMatrix{T<:Complex} -> AbstractMatrix{T<:Complex}`, type stable.
2.2 [OPEN] Literature survey for algorithms for cube roots of triangular matrices from 1983 -- 2023.
2.3 Known option (1983): Also as you mention, a method is provided in [1, Section 5] using similar principles as the square-root method.

3. Arbitrary real-valued matrices:
3.1 Using Schur decomposition: `cbrt :: AbstractMatrix{T1<:Real} -> AbstractMatrix{T2}`. Outputs of Schur decomposition are: (a) triangular for matrices with real-valued eigenvalues, and (b) quasi-triangular for matrices with complex-valued eigenvalues.
3.2 For matrices with real-valued eigenvalues, utilise a real-valued version of the algorithm in Step 2 above. In this case, the output matrix is real-valued.
3.3 **[APPROACH 1]** For matrices with complex-valued eigenvalues, convert the quasi-triangular output to complex-valued triangular via Given's rotations, see `function Schur{CT}(S::Schur{<:Real}) where {CT<:Complex}` in `schur.jl`, and utilise the algorithm in Step 2 for complex-valued matrices. This approach is **type unstable** since the output matrix is complex-valued.
3.4 **[APPROACH 2]** For matrices with complex-valued eigenvalues, implement a cube-root function for a quasi-triangular matrix, which can be adapted to return real-valued results. This approach is type stable since the output matrix is real-valued. However, a quick search revealed no cube root algorithms for quasi-triangular (2x2 blocks on the diagonal) matrices. An algorithm can surely be developed but might take some time to get right.
3.5 **[APPROACH 3, Not elegant at all!]** For matrices with complex-valued eigenvalues, return an error and force the user to wrap the matrix in `complex`, see the first inconsistency below. This approach is type stable.

[1] Åke Björck, Sven Hammarling, A Schur method for the square root of a matrix, Linear Algebra and its Applications, Volumes 52–53, 1983, Pages 127-140, ISSN 0024-3795, https://doi.org/10.1016/0024-3795(83)80010-X.

Lastly, while reviewing the code, I found a few inconsistencies:

1. `sqrt` behaviour is non-intuitive. Consider:
```julia
julia> using LinearAlgebra
julia> sqrt(Diagonal([-1. 0; 0 1.]))
ERROR: DomainError with -1.0:
sqrt was called with a negative real argument but will only [...]
```
but

```julia
julia> sqrt([-1. 0; 0 1.])
2×2 Matrix{ComplexF64}:
 0.0+1.0im  0.0+0.0im
 0.0+0.0im  1.0+0.0im
```
(Note: There are several other inconsistencies. I'll just stop here.)

2. `sqrt` dies silently for rank-deficient matrices:
```julia
julia> using LinearAlgebra
julia> sqrt([0 1; 0 0])
2×2 Matrix{Float64}:
 0.0  0.0
 0.0  0.0
```
Perhaps showing a warning or an error would be better here.

on my revised reading of the requirements of this issue, taking into consideration the latest post by the author (@stevengj), please find below a summary of the goal of this issue and a plan.

# Goal
Akin to scalar values, cube-root of a real-valued matrix can be arranged to be real-valued. In Julia, presently, cube-root of a matrix via `A^(1//3)` is not guaranteed to return real-valued outputs for real-valued inputs. Hence, the goals of this issue are as follows:
1. Provide a function `cbrt :: AbstractMatrix{<:Real} -> AbstractMatrix{<:Real}`, which provides real-valued outputs for real-valued inputs.
2. On the other hand, this issue is not concerned with `cbrt :: AbstractMatrix{<:Complex} -> AbstractMatrix{<:Complex}`, which can just be delegated to `A^(1//3)`, as indicated in the issue text.

# Plan
## 1. Diagonal, symmetric, and Hermitian matrices
- [ ] Diagonal matrices: `cbrt :: Diagonal{T<:Real} -> Diagonal{T}`, can be made type stable.
- [ ] Symmetric matrices: `cbrt :: Symmetric{T<:Real} -> Symmetric{T}`, can be made type stable.
- [ ] Hermitian-symmetric matrices: `cbrt :: Hermitian{T<:Complex} -> Hermitian{T<:Complex}`, delegate to `A^(1//3)`.

### Implementation notes
As indicated above by the OP, the scalar `cbrt` function returns real-valued outputs for real-valued inputs. Hence, the implementations of Point 1. above can be based on `cbrt` of the diagonal or eigenvalues. 

**TODO:**
- [ ] Benchmark `eigen` and `schur` based implementations for symmetric and Hermitian matrices as a function of the matrix dimension to identify the most efficient implementation.

## 2. Arbitrary complex-valued matrices:
- [ ] Abstract matrices: `cbrt :: AbstractMatrix{T<:Complex} -> AbstractMatrix{T}`, type stable, delegated to `A^(1//3)`.

## 3. Arbitrary real-valued matrices:
- [ ] Abstract matrices: `cbrt :: AbstractMatrix{T<:Real} -> AbstractMatrix{T}`, can be made type stable.

### Implementation notes
Except for the algorithm indicated by OP in [1], a quick search revealed no literature from $1983 - 2023$ for a real-valued to real-valued cube root of matrices. Schur-decomposition based implementation is preferred here as, unlike `eigen`, `schur` can handle defective matrices. However, Schur-based implementation necessitates finding the cube-root of a quasi-triangular matrix, which might be cumbersome.

**Preparation:**
- [ ] Review the cube root algorithm in [1] in detail and **extend the method for quasi-triangular matrices**, which are are obtained for input matrices with complex eigenvalues.
- [ ] Review literature in the period $1983 - 2023$ for applicable algorithms.

# Overall TODOs
- [ ] Ensure graceful handling of rank-deficient matrices (error or warning messages).

[1] Åke Björck, Sven Hammarling, A Schur method for the square root of a matrix, Linear Algebra and its Applications, Volumes 52–53, 1983, Pages 127-140, ISSN 0024-3795, https://doi.org/10.1016/0024-3795(83)80010-X.

# Summary
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The function `eigen!(A,B)` when either of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition, which is only valid for positive definite matrix `B`. Hence, the function fails for Hermitian or symmetric `B`.

# Changes
1. Include definitions for `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` and `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` which utilise the generic (dense) matrix variants.

2. Change the definitions of  `function eigen!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` and `function eigen!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` to utilise the generic (dense) matrix variants.

3. Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, C::Cholesky{T, <:AbstractMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which can take advantage of Cholesky decomposition to reduce the computational complexity of `B` is positive definite.

4. Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, B::BunchKaufman{T,<:StridedMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which tan take advantage of Bunchkaufman (LDLT) decomposition to reduce the computational complexity if `B` is Hermitian or symmetric.

# Plan
- [X] `function eigen!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigen!(Matrix{T}(A), B; sortby)`

- [X] `function eigen!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigen!(A, Matrix{T}(B); sortby)`

- [X] `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigvals!(A, Matrix{T}(B); sortby)`

- [X] Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, C::Cholesky{T, <:AbstractMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which can take advantage of Cholesky decomposition to reduce the computational complexity of `B` is positive definite.

- [X] Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, B::BunchKaufman{T,<:StridedMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which tan take advantage of Bunchkaufman (LDLT) decomposition to reduce the computational complexity if `B` is Hermitian or symmetric.

- [X] Add unit tests.

# Notes
1. The Cholesky and Bunchkaufman decompostion based versions are only efficient if the matrix dimension $N > 1000.$ For smaller matrices, the generic (dense) variant is better. See below for benchmarks.

# TODO
- [ ] File an issue on `tridiagonal.jl` to support `HermTridiagonal` and `ldlt` for `HermTridiagonal`.

PR contains a fix for #49533.

# Summary
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The function `eigen!(A,B)` when either of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition, which is only valid for positive definite matrix `B`. Hence, the function fails for Hermitian or symmetric `B`.

# Changes
1. Include definitions for `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` and `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` which utilise the generic (dense) matrix variants.

2. Change the definitions of  `function eigen!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` and `function eigen!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` to utilise the generic (dense) matrix variants.

3. Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, C::Cholesky{T, <:AbstractMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which can take advantage of Cholesky decomposition to reduce the computational complexity of `B` is positive definite.

4. Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, B::BunchKaufman{T,<:StridedMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which tan take advantage of Bunchkaufman (LDLT) decomposition to reduce the computational complexity if `B` is Hermitian or symmetric.

# Plan
- [X] `function eigen!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigen!(Matrix{T}(A), B; sortby)`

- [X] `function eigen!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigen!(A, Matrix{T}(B); sortby)`

- [X] `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigvals!(A, Matrix{T}(B); sortby)`

- [X] `function eigvals!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigvals!(Matrix{T}(A), B; sortby)`

- [X] Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, C::Cholesky{T, <:AbstractMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which can take advantage of Cholesky decomposition to reduce the computational complexity of `B` is positive definite.

- [X] Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, B::BunchKaufman{T,<:StridedMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which tan take advantage of Bunchkaufman (LDLT) decomposition to reduce the computational complexity if `B` is Hermitian or symmetric.

- [X] Add unit tests.

# Notes
1. The Cholesky and Bunchkaufman decompostion based versions are only efficient if the matrix dimension $N > 1000.$ For smaller matrices, the generic (dense) variant is better. See below for benchmarks.

# TODO
- [ ] File an issue on `tridiagonal.jl` to support `HermTridiagonal` and `ldlt` for `HermTridiagonal`.
- [ ] File an issue on `bunchkaufman` to return `SymTridiagonal` or `HermTridiagonal` instead of `Tridiagonal`. Then, `ldlt` can be exploited to speed up Bunchkaufman-based implementation.

PR contains a fix for #49533.

# Summary
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The function `eigen!(A,B)` when either of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition, which is only valid for positive definite matrix `B`. Hence, the function fails for Hermitian or symmetric `B`.

# Changes
1. Include definitions for `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` and `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` which utilise the generic (dense) matrix variants.

2. Change the definitions of  `function eigen!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` and `function eigen!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` to utilise the generic (dense) matrix variants.

3. Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, C::Cholesky{T, <:AbstractMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which can take advantage of Cholesky decomposition to reduce the computational complexity of `B` is positive definite.

4. Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, B::BunchKaufman{T,<:StridedMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which tan take advantage of Bunchkaufman (LDLT) decomposition to reduce the computational complexity if `B` is Hermitian or symmetric.

# Plan
- [X] `function eigen!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigen!(Matrix{T}(A), B; sortby)`

- [X] `function eigen!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigen!(A, Matrix{T}(B); sortby)`

- [X] `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigvals!(A, Matrix{T}(B); sortby)`

- [X] `function eigvals!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigvals!(Matrix{T}(A), B; sortby)`

- [X] Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, C::Cholesky{T, <:AbstractMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which can take advantage of Cholesky decomposition to reduce the computational complexity of `B` is positive definite.

- [X] Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, B::BunchKaufman{T,<:StridedMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which tan take advantage of Bunchkaufman (LDLT) decomposition to reduce the computational complexity if `B` is Hermitian or symmetric.

- [X] Add unit tests.

# Notes
1. The Cholesky and Bunchkaufman decompostion based versions are only efficient if the matrix dimension $N > 1000.$ For smaller matrices, the generic (dense) variant is better. See below for benchmarks.

# TODO
- [ ] File an issue on `tridiagonal.jl` to support `HermTridiagonal` and `ldlt` for `HermTridiagonal`.
- [ ] File an issue on `bunchkaufman` to return `SymTridiagonal` or `HermTridiagonal` instead of `Tridiagonal`. Then, `ldlt` can be exploited to speed up Bunchkaufman-based implementation.

PR contains a fix for #49533.

# Summary
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The function `eigen!(A,B)` when either of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition, which is only valid for positive definite matrix `B`. Hence, the function fails for Hermitian or symmetric `B`.

# Changes
1. Include definitions for `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` and `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` which utilise the generic (dense) matrix variants.

2. Change the definitions of  `function eigen!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` and `function eigen!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` to utilise the generic (dense) matrix variants.

3. Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, C::Cholesky{T, <:AbstractMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which can take advantage of Cholesky decomposition to reduce the computational complexity of `B` is positive definite.

4. Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, B::BunchKaufman{T,<:StridedMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which tan take advantage of Bunchkaufman (LDLT) decomposition to reduce the computational complexity if `B` is Hermitian or symmetric.

# Plan
- [X] `function eigen!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigen!(Matrix{T}(A), B; sortby)`

- [X] `function eigen!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigen!(A, Matrix{T}(B); sortby)`

- [X] `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigvals!(A, Matrix{T}(B); sortby)`

- [X] `function eigvals!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigvals!(Matrix{T}(A), B; sortby)`

- [X] Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, C::Cholesky{T, <:AbstractMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which can take advantage of Cholesky decomposition to reduce the computational complexity of `B` is positive definite.

- [X] Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, B::BunchKaufman{T,<:StridedMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which tan take advantage of Bunchkaufman (LDLT) decomposition to reduce the computational complexity if `B` is Hermitian or symmetric.

- [X] Add unit tests.

# Notes
1. The Cholesky and Bunchkaufman decompostion based versions are only efficient if the matrix dimension $N > 1000.$ For smaller matrices, the generic (dense) variant is better. See below for benchmarks.

# TODO
- [ ] File an issue on `tridiagonal.jl` to support `HermTridiagonal` and `ldlt` for `HermTridiagonal`.
- [ ] File an issue on `bunchkaufman` to return `SymTridiagonal` or `HermTridiagonal` instead of `Tridiagonal`. Then, `ldlt` can be exploited to speed up Bunchkaufman-based implementation.

PR contains a fix for #49533.

# Summary
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The function `eigen!(A,B)` when either of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition, which is only valid for positive definite matrix `B`. Hence, the function fails for Hermitian or symmetric `B`.

# Changes
1. Include definitions for `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` and `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` which utilise the generic (dense) matrix variants.

2. Change the definitions of  `function eigen!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` and `function eigen!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` to utilise the generic (dense) matrix variants.

3. Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, C::Cholesky{T, <:AbstractMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which can take advantage of Cholesky decomposition to reduce the computational complexity of `B` is positive definite.

4. Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, B::BunchKaufman{T,<:StridedMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which tan take advantage of Bunchkaufman (LDLT) decomposition to reduce the computational complexity if `B` is Hermitian or symmetric.

# Plan
- [X] `function eigen!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigen!(Matrix{T}(A), B; sortby)`

- [X] `function eigen!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigen!(A, Matrix{T}(B); sortby)`

- [X] `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigvals!(A, Matrix{T}(B); sortby)`

- [X] `function eigvals!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigvals!(Matrix{T}(A), B; sortby)`

- [X] Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, C::Cholesky{T, <:AbstractMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which can take advantage of Cholesky decomposition to reduce the computational complexity of `B` is positive definite.

- [X] Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, B::BunchKaufman{T,<:StridedMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which tan take advantage of Bunchkaufman (LDLT) decomposition to reduce the computational complexity if `B` is Hermitian or symmetric.

- [X] Add unit tests.

# Notes
1. The Cholesky and Bunchkaufman decompostion based versions are only efficient if the matrix dimension $N > 1000.$ For smaller matrices, the generic (dense) variant is better. See below for benchmarks.

# TODO
- [ ] File an issue on `tridiagonal.jl` to support `HermTridiagonal` and `ldlt` for `HermTridiagonal`.
- [ ] File an issue on `bunchkaufman` to return `SymTridiagonal` or `HermTridiagonal` instead of `Tridiagonal`. Then, `ldlt` can be exploited to speed up Bunchkaufman-based implementation.

PR contains a fix for #49533.

# Summary
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The function `eigen!(A,B)` when either of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition, which is only valid for positive definite matrix `B`. Hence, the function fails for Hermitian or symmetric `B`.

# Changes
1. Include definitions for `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` and `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` which utilise the generic (dense) matrix variants.

2. Change the definitions of  `function eigen!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` and `function eigen!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` to utilise the generic (dense) matrix variants.

3. Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, C::Cholesky{T, <:AbstractMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which can take advantage of Cholesky decomposition to reduce the computational complexity of `B` is positive definite.

4. Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, B::BunchKaufman{T,<:StridedMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which tan take advantage of Bunchkaufman (LDLT) decomposition to reduce the computational complexity if `B` is Hermitian or symmetric.

# Plan
- [X] `function eigen!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigen!(Matrix{T}(A), B; sortby)`

- [X] `function eigen!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigen!(A, Matrix{T}(B); sortby)`

- [X] `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigvals!(A, Matrix{T}(B); sortby)`

- [X] `function eigvals!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigvals!(Matrix{T}(A), B; sortby)`

- [X] Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, C::Cholesky{T, <:AbstractMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which can take advantage of Cholesky decomposition to reduce the computational complexity of `B` is positive definite.

- [X] Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, B::BunchKaufman{T,<:StridedMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which tan take advantage of Bunchkaufman (LDLT) decomposition to reduce the computational complexity if `B` is Hermitian or symmetric.

- [X] Add unit tests.

# Notes
1. The Cholesky and Bunchkaufman decompostion based versions are only efficient if the matrix dimension $N > 1000.$ For smaller matrices, the generic (dense) variant is better. See below for benchmarks.

# TODO
- [ ] File an issue on `tridiagonal.jl` to support `HermTridiagonal` and `ldlt` for `HermTridiagonal`.

PR contains a fix for #49533.

# Summary
1. No methods are defined for the case `eigenvals!(A,B)` when one of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric.
2. The function `eigen!(A,B)` when either of `A` or `B` is not (Hermitian or) symmetric, computes the solution based on Cholesky decomposition, which is only valid for positive definite matrix `B`. Hence, the function fails for Hermitian or symmetric `B`.

# Changes
1. Include definitions for `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` and `function eigvals!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` which utilise the generic (dense) matrix variants.

2. Change the definitions of  `function eigen!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` and `function eigen!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` to utilise the generic (dense) matrix variants.

3. Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, C::Cholesky{T, <:AbstractMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which can take advantage of Cholesky decomposition to reduce the computational complexity of `B` is positive definite.

4. Define a new function `function eigvals(A::AbstractMatrix{T}, B::BunchKaufman{T,<:StridedMatrix}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}`, which tan take advantage of Bunchkaufman (LDLT) decomposition to reduce the computational complexity if `B` is Hermitian or symmetric.

# Plan
- [X] `function eigen!(A::RealHermSymComplexHerm{T,<:StridedMatrix}, B::AbstractMatrix{T}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigen!(Matrix{T}(A), B; sortby)`

- [X] `function eigen!(A::StridedMatrix{T}, B::Union{RealHermSymComplexHerm{T},Diagonal{T}}; sortby::Union{Function,Nothing}=nothing) where {T<:Number}` is forwarded to `eigen!(A, Matrix{T}(B); sortby)`
